This real-world operational data reinforces the need to equip HVAC systems with optimization systems that can effectively evaluate internal and ambient conditions and automatically adjust system setpoints to minimize energy waste. Control strategies that over-emphasize energy savings, however, can have negative consequences for comfort, so it is critical to ensure a balance between saving energy and meeting the comfort needs of building occupants. Occupant complaints may be handled by the operating engineers by manually overriding the fan systems and the cooling and heating system setpoints, which can eliminate the energy efficiency benefits of an optimization system. It is noted that the baseline operating conditions used during the M&V were selected to reflect how real CAV and VAV systems are often operated. If a Building Management System (BMS) or Direct Digital Control (DDC) system is not in use, or it is not equipped with some form of an after-market, 3rd party HVAC optimization platform that covers the chillers, boilers, AHUs and cooling towers (if so equipped), and their associated pumping systems, for example in a legacy HVAC system, it is not uncommon for facility operators to configure the HVAC system so that it continues to operate the cooling coil to control to a fixed supply air dry bulb temperature setpoint, and allow the heating system to control the temperature in the conditioned spaces, particularly for a temperature and humidity sensitive application such as a museum. The HVAC operation may be modified manually during different seasons or when there is a significant and enduring change in weather conditions, but if active controls are not in place to automatically adjust the setpoints in real time, it is generally considered too burdensome for the facility operator to regularly make changes to operating setpoints as weather, building occupancy and other conditions change at the facility. 22 This report is available at no cost from NREL at www.nrel.gov/publications. While the CAV and VAV baseline operation modes evaluated represent a realistic reference case to compare the HEDS operation against, it is also important to consider a reference case that is consistent with modern standards (at least since 2010) that prohibit simultaneous cooling and reheating for zone control. For this reason, we created an alternate baseline case that includes automatic resets to comply with code requirements, as described in the following sections. 2.2.3 Conclusions Regarding System Operation During the CAV and VAV Baseline M&V Conditions (Operating Periods 3 and 5) for the Winter Evaluation The results from the winter evaluation period highlighted that typical non-optimized baseline HVAC system operation, in both VAV and CAV modes, is very wasteful. The baseline energy use in modern, code compliant HVAC systems that are equipped with control software that reduces the level of energy waste will be lower than the measured baselines.
